title: Equal in deeds
hookLine: the four castes are equal before their own deeds

cards: This conversation happens after the Buddha has died. His disciple Mahākaccāna, a monk remembered for opening up short teachings at length, is staying in a grove near the city of Madhurā.
The king of Madhurā comes to see him with a question that's been circulating.
Some brahmins of that time held that their class was the highest: born from Brahmā's own mouth, fair where others were dark, pure where others weren't. What does the monk say to that?
Mahākaccāna doesn't answer with a slogan. He asks the king to look at how the world actually works.

teach.b: Society at the time was described in four classes: nobles and warriors, brahmins or priests, merchants, and laborers. Mahākaccāna takes them one test at a time. First, money.
If a noble becomes rich, will people of every class rise before him, run his errands, speak pleasantly to win his favor? Yes, says the king. And if a laborer becomes rich?
The same. Then in this, the four classes are equal. Second, conduct.
If a person of any class kills, steals, lies, what happens after death, as you understand it? Rebirth in a bad state, whatever their class. And if they live well?
A good rebirth, whatever their class. Equal again. Third, the law.
If a thief is caught breaking into a house, does your court ask his class before punishing him? No.
The same punishment for all. Fourth, the spiritual life.
If someone of any class shaves their head, goes forth and lives well, do you honor them as a monk?
Yes, the king says, whatever their birth. Test after test, the same answer. Mahākaccāna isn't saying everyone is identical, or that background doesn't shape a life.
He's saying that when it counts, in what people do and what follows from it, birth doesn't settle anything. At the end, the king asks where the Buddha is now. He has passed away, Mahākaccāna says.
And the king goes for refuge to the Buddha who has passed, the teaching, and the community. The teacher was gone; the teaching was still answering questions.

how: Buddhist monastic communities ordain people of any background, and seniority among monks and nuns is counted from the day of ordination, not from birth or family.

games.q: Mahākaccāna's four tests: tap the pairs.
p: everyone serves the rich, whatever class
a thief of any class is punished

s: this conversation takes place during the Buddha's lifetime
it's after his death; the king takes refuge in the Buddha who has passed.
Mahākaccāna answers by asking the king questions
four tests, each answered by the king himself.
the sutta claims everyone's life is identical, whatever their background
it says birth doesn't settle what matters: deeds and their results.

games.q: you're the king's judge. a thief is caught breaking into a house. what do you ask first?
o: what class he was born into
games.why: the king admits the law punishes a thief of any class the same way. Mahākaccāna: then in this, the four are equal.

practice: Picture the people you'll meet: someone serving you coffee, someone senior at work, someone sleeping in a doorway, someone in a nice car. Notice any small shift in how you'd greet each one, without scolding yourself.
Then picture greeting each with the same eyes and the same voice, and breathe with that.

wordCard.voice: Vanna. Mahākaccāna's four tests, money, conduct, the law and going forth, and the same answer each time: birth doesn't settle it.

orig.note: Pali vaṇṇa (Sanskrit varṇa): color, class. the four vaṇṇas are the four social classes the sutta discusses.

carryVoice: Your line: not by birth. In what people do, the four classes come out equal. That's day four hundred seventy.
